title: Net Worth by Age in 2026: Where Do You Rank?

scenes.narration: Be honest. You've looked at your bank account and wondered the same thing everyone does: am I ahead, or am I behind for my age? It turns out there's an actual answer — measured, every few years, by the Federal Reserve. And the number that counts as perfectly normal at each age is going to surprise you.

Let's rip the band-aid off. The typical American under thirty-five has a net worth of about thirty-nine thousand dollars. Not thirty-nine thousand in savings — thirty-nine thousand total, everything they own minus everything they owe.

If that feels low, that's the point. Most people wildly overestimate where everyone else is. Social media shows you the winners. The Fed shows you reality. So today, let's find out exactly where you rank — at every age, with the real numbers.

scenes.memeBottom: than whether it's bigger than last year's
scenes.narration: And stick around to the end, because the real lesson isn't about beating other people. It's a single number you should actually be chasing — and it has almost nothing to do with your age.
First, two quick rules so these numbers actually mean something.
scenes.heading: Reading the Numbers

scenes.narration: Rule one: everything here is net worth — the value of all your assets, minus the value of all your outstanding liabilities. Your house, car, savings, and investments, minus every debt you carry.

Rule two: we use the median, not the average. The median is the value separating the higher half from the lower half — the person smack in the middle. It's the honest number, because it isn't skewed by a handful of billionaires.

This matters enormously. The average, or mean, American under thirty-five looks rich — about a hundred and eighty-four thousand dollars. But that's a lie told by a few mega-fortunes dragging the average up. The median — the real middle person — is that humble thirty-nine thousand.
scenes.caption: why the 'average' lies

scenes.narration: This is exactly why everyone feels poor. You see one friend with a new Tesla and assume you're hopelessly behind. But you're comparing your real, median life to someone else's highlight reel — or to a skewed average puffed up by a few billionaires. The honest comparison almost always says you're more normal than you feel.
And all of this comes from the Survey of Consumer Finances — a detailed statistical survey of the balance sheet of American families, run by the Federal Reserve. It's the gold standard for this data.
Now the big idea that makes comparing yourself to others mostly pointless.
scenes.heading: The Life-Cycle Hump

scenes.narration: Economists have a model for this called the life-cycle hypothesis — a model that tries to explain the consumption patterns of individuals across their whole life. In short: you borrow when young, save in middle age, and spend it down in retirement.

So net worth isn't flat. It's a hump. It starts near zero in your twenties, climbs steadily through your working years, peaks right around retirement, and then gently declines as you spend your savings. Comparing a twenty-five-year-old to a sixty-year-old is comparing two totally different points on this curve.
scenes.caption: wealth is a life-cycle hump

scenes.narration: So never compare your number to someone a decade older. Of course a fifty-five-year-old has more than you — they've had twenty extra years on the curve. The only fair comparisons are to people exactly your age, and to your own self, last year.

scenes.title: Median net worth by age ($ thousands)
scenes.narration: Here's the whole hump in real Fed numbers. Thirty-nine thousand under thirty-five. A hundred thirty-five thousand in your late thirties and early forties. Two hundred forty-seven thousand in your late forties. Three hundred sixty-five thousand approaching retirement, peaking near four hundred ten thousand in your late sixties.

And here's what hides inside these numbers: for the typical family, the bulk of that net worth isn't a brokerage account — it's home equity. Their house, slowly paid down over decades, is the single biggest brick in the pile. Which is why owning where you live is still the default road to middle-class wealth.
Let's walk up the curve, decade by decade, and see where you stand.
scenes.heading: Your 20s & Early 30s

scenes.narration: Under thirty-five, the median is thirty-nine thousand — but this group is wildly spread out. A huge share are at zero or negative, buried under student loans and car payments. If you've simply clawed your way to a positive net worth in your twenties, you are genuinely ahead of the pack.

At this age, the actual dollar amount barely matters. What matters is the habit. The twenty-five-year-old who invests two hundred dollars a month is quietly building a machine that will out-earn almost any amount of frantic catch-up later. This is the cheapest, most powerful decade you'll ever get.

To see why your twenties are pure gold, look at a single dollar. One dollar invested at twenty-five can become roughly fifteen dollars by sixty-five. The same dollar invested at forty-five becomes only about four. Your young dollars aren't just dollars — they're seeds with decades to grow.
scenes.sub: what $1 invested at age 25 becomes by 65

scenes.narration: Add a decade, and the picture changes fast.
scenes.heading: Your Late 30s & 40s

scenes.narration: From thirty-five to forty-four, the median jumps to about a hundred thirty-five thousand. This is the accumulation decade — careers peak, salaries rise, and for most people a house quietly becomes their single biggest asset. The hump officially starts climbing.

But this is also the decade of the great squeeze. Mortgages, childcare, and keeping up with the neighbors devour the income. Plenty of people earning serious money still have a thin net worth here — because it's all flowing straight back out the door.

And not all of that debt is a disaster. A mortgage on a home that appreciates, or a loan for a skill that lifts your income, can be genuinely good debt. The real killer is the other kind — high-interest credit cards and car loans on things that only lose value. Kill those first, with a vengeance.
Now we hit the decade where the gap between people explodes.
scenes.heading: Your 40s & 50s

scenes.narration: From forty-five to fifty-four, the median hits about two hundred forty-seven thousand. These are usually your peak earning years — and the compounding you started decades ago is finally doing visible, heavy lifting. For savers, net worth can now jump by tens of thousands a year on its own.

Watch what that compounding actually does. A hundred thousand dollars invested at age forty-five, left completely alone at a normal market return, can quietly grow past three hundred thousand by the time you retire — without you adding another single cent.

scenes.memeBottom: own assets that quietly grow while you earn the salary
scenes.narration: And this is where the two types of people visibly split. One has a big salary and a small net worth. The other has let assets quietly compound for twenty years — and is now pulling away, fast, almost without effort.
Approaching the finish line, the hump reaches its peak.
scenes.heading: Your 50s & 60s

scenes.narration: From fifty-five to sixty-four, the median climbs to around three hundred sixty-five thousand, peaking near four hundred ten thousand in the late sixties. This is the top of the hump — the moment of truth, when decades of saving either add up to a comfortable retirement, or they don't.

Now, it's not quite as scary as it sounds, because most retirees also collect Social Security — a monthly check from the government. But for an average earner, that replaces only around forty percent of their old paycheck. It's a floor, not a hammock. Your own savings still have to do the heavy lifting.

After this, net worth usually falls — because retirement is, by definition, the withdrawal from one's active working life. You stop earning and start spending down the pile you spent forty years building.

And here's the sobering part: for most households, that peak of around four hundred thousand dollars is dangerously thin for a thirty-year retirement. A huge slice of Americans arrive at sixty-five with far too little — which is exactly why knowing these numbers early matters so much.

Run the famous four-percent rule on that peak. A four-hundred-thousand-dollar nest egg safely throws off only about sixteen thousand dollars a year. Add Social Security on top and it's survivable — but it is nobody's dream retirement.
scenes.sub: a year from a $400K nest egg (the 4% rule)

scenes.narration: So you've seen the medians. But a median only tells you the middle. How do you actually rank?
scenes.heading: Where Do You Rank?

scenes.narration: Think of everyone your age lined up from poorest to richest. The median is the person dead center — the fiftieth percentile. If you've got double the median for your age, you're knocking on the top twenty-five percent. Hit roughly five times the median, and you're brushing the top ten.
scenes.caption: where do you rank, for your age?

scenes.narration: And if you're wondering what truly elite looks like: the top one percent threshold climbs with age too. For younger households it's a couple of million. By your sixties, cracking the top one percent takes well over ten million dollars. The ceiling rises just as fast as the floor.

scenes.title: Median vs. average net worth by age ($K)
scenes.narration: And watch the gap between the median and the average balloon with age. Under thirty-five, the average is around a hundred eighty-four thousand versus a median of thirty-nine. By your late fifties, the average rockets past one and a half million — while the median sits near three hundred sixty-five thousand. The rich pull away harder every decade.
Chasing a percentile can feel hopeless. So here's a far better target.
scenes.heading: A Cleaner Target

scenes.narration: Instead of a raw dollar amount, aim for a multiple of your own salary. A popular benchmark says: have one times your salary saved by thirty, three times by forty, six times by fifty, eight times by sixty, and ten times by sixty-seven. It scales to your life, not a stranger's.
scenes.caption: a cleaner target: multiples of your salary

scenes.narration: This is so much fairer than a flat number. Someone earning fifty thousand and someone earning two hundred thousand need wildly different piles to retire. The multiple adjusts automatically — it asks not 'are you rich?' but 'are you on track for your own life?'

Make it concrete. If you earn sixty thousand dollars a year, your targets are simple: sixty thousand saved by thirty, a hundred eighty thousand by forty, three hundred sixty thousand by fifty. Suddenly the vague question 'where should I be?' has a real, personal answer.
But there's an elephant in the room. Why does it feel so much harder than it did for your parents?
scenes.heading: The Generation Gap

scenes.narration: Because it genuinely is harder. Compared to earlier generations at the same age, younger people today face far pricier homes, mountains of student debt, and wages that haven't kept pace. Feeling behind isn't always a personal failing — sometimes the track itself got steeper.

And the wealth itself is lopsided by generation. Baby boomers alone hold roughly half of all the wealth in the country. Gen X holds a chunk, Millennials a sliver, and Gen Z barely a rounding error — and that gap is wider than age alone can explain.
scenes.caption: share of US wealth, by generation

scenes.narration: And dig into the why, and it's not avocado toast. Since the eighties, home prices have far outrun wages, the cost of college exploded, and secure pensions quietly vanished. Younger generations are running the very same race — on a track that genuinely got steeper and more expensive.

Who are the boomers hogging all of it? The demographic cohort of people born from 1946 to 1964 — the huge generation that bought homes cheap, rode decades of rising markets, and now sits on most of the nation's assets.

This isn't your imagination, either. Wealth inequality has substantially increased in the United States since the late 1980s — the top has pulled away from everyone else, and the young are furthest from the top.

There is one twist on the horizon. As the boomers age, tens of trillions of dollars are set to pass down — the biggest wealth transfer in history. Some younger people will inherit a fortune. Most won't — which makes quietly building your own, from scratch, matter more than ever.
So if the track is steeper and the numbers are daunting, what actually works?
scenes.heading: The One Real Lever

scenes.narration: The answer is the quiet engine behind every one of these numbers: compound interest — interest accumulated on a principal sum and on previously accumulated interest. It rewards one thing above all else: time in the market.

Look at what a ten-year head start does. Someone who starts saving at twenty-five, versus someone who starts the exact same amount at thirty-five, can end up with nearly double the money by sixty-five. Same effort — the early starter just gave compounding an extra decade to work.
scenes.caption: the one asset you can't buy back: time

scenes.narration: Put a price tag on procrastination. Delaying your investing by just ten years can cost you hundreds of thousands of dollars by retirement — not because you invested any less, but purely because you gave that money less time. Waiting is quietly the most expensive thing you can do.
scenes.sub: the price of waiting 10 years to start

scenes.memeTop: wait until I earn more to start investing
scenes.memeBottom: lose the one thing money can't buy back — a decade
scenes.narration: This is why 'I'll start investing once I earn more' is the most expensive sentence in personal finance. The dollars you invest in your twenties are worth far more than the dollars you'll invest in your forties — because they get decades more to grow.
So let's turn all of this into what you should actually do tomorrow morning.
scenes.heading: What To Do

scenes.narration: First, stop comparing yourself to other people and other ages. The only scoreboard that matters is you, last year. Is your net worth higher than it was twelve months ago? Then you won. That's the entire game, repeated.

So actually measure it. Once a year, on your birthday, add up everything you own, subtract everything you owe, and write that one number down. That single habit — just watching the line move — quietly turns vague money anxiety into a plan you can actually win.

Second, aim for the salary multiples, not the headlines. One times your salary by thirty, three times by forty. They're concrete, personal, and completely achievable on an ordinary income — if you start, and you stay consistent.

Third, and most important: start now, whatever your age. The best time to plant the tree was twenty years ago. The second best time is this afternoon. Every single day you wait hands a little more of your future wealth to the person who didn't.

And if you're in your fifties and feel hopelessly behind — you're not. The tax system actually rewards you with bigger catch-up contributions after fifty. A determined decade of aggressive saving can still rescue a retirement. The one truly fatal move is deciding it's too late and giving up.

Because here's the truth hiding under all these charts. Your net worth by age isn't really a test you pass or fail. It's a trajectory. And the only question that actually matters is whether that line, however low it starts, is pointed up.

youtube.hook: Am I ahead or behind for my age? Here's the real answer, from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances. We break down median net worth by age — $39K under 35, $135K at 35–44, $247K at 45–54, peaking near $410K at 65–74 — and why you must use the median, not the skewed average. Then: the life-cycle hump, the 'where do you rank' percentiles, a far better target than a flat dollar amount (salary multiples: 1x by 30, 3x by 40, 6x by 50, 8x by 60, 10x by 67), the brutal generational wealth gap (boomers hold ~half of everything), and the one lever that beats all of it — starting early, because a 10-year head start can nearly double your finish. Fully cited.
